nameStory: The Norway maple gets its name from its native range, which includes Norway and much of northern Europe. Despite being called a "Norway" maple, this tree actually grows across a vast area from Spain all the way to Russia! It was brought to North America in the mid-1700s by European settlers who valued it as a fast-growing shade tree.
description: Norway maple is a large deciduous tree that can grow 40-60 feet tall with a broad, rounded crown. It's an introduced species from Europe that has become very common in New England's urban and suburban areas. The tree has a sturdy trunk and creates dense shade with its full canopy of large, broad leaves. In spring, it produces clusters of small yellowish-green flowers before the leaves emerge.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large palmate leaves (hand-shaped) with 5 pointed lobes and few teeth along the edges. The leaves feel thick and sturdy, almost leathery, and when you break the leaf stem, a milky white sap oozes out - this is the Norway maple's signature feature.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellowish-green flowers appear in showy upright clusters in early spring before leaves emerge. Each small flower has 5 petals and creates a distinctive chartreuse glow on the bare branches that's visible from a distance.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Winged seeds called samaras hang in pairs with wings spread very wide apart (almost in a straight line). The seeds are large and flat, and the wings help them helicopter to the ground in late summer.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Gray-brown bark that becomes furrowed with age, developing interlacing ridges that create a diamond-like pattern. Young bark is smoother and lighter gray.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Dense, rounded crown that casts very heavy shade. Branches are sturdy and spread wide, often creating a broad canopy that's wider than the tree is tall.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Large, plump reddish-brown buds that are noticeably bigger than native maple buds. Winter buds are arranged opposite each other on the branch and have a rounded, almost bulbous appearance.

habitat: Norway maples thrive in urban and suburban areas throughout New England, tolerating air pollution, compacted soil, and road salt better than most native trees. You'll commonly find them planted along streets, in parks, and around homes, but they also escape cultivation and establish in forest edges and disturbed areas. They prefer well-drained soils but adapt to various conditions from dry to moist.

seasonality.spring: Showy yellowish-green flower clusters bloom in early April before leaves emerge, creating a distinctive chartreuse glow. New leaves unfurl soon after, appearing bronze-green before turning deep green.
seasonality.summer: Dense canopy of large, dark green leaves provides heavy shade. Look for the thick, leathery leaf texture and remember to break a leaf stem to see the telltale milky sap.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn bright yellow, sometimes with orange tones, usually later than native maples. The fall color is often more uniform and less varied than sugar maples.
seasonality.winter: Large, plump reddish-brown buds are distinctive, along with the furrowed bark pattern. Dead samaras may persist on branches, and the broad branching pattern is visible.

funFact: Norway maple leaves stay green much later in fall than native maples, and their roots release chemicals that inhibit the growth of other plants underneath - this is why you rarely see anything growing under a mature Norway maple except bare soil!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with sugar maple, but the milky sap trick never fails - break a Norway maple leaf stem and white sap oozes out, while sugar maple stems have clear sap. Memory trick: "Norway = no other plants below" due to the bare ground underneath mature trees.
contextualKnowledge: Though widely planted and naturalized, Norway maple is considered invasive in many New England areas because it outcompetes native trees and creates biological deserts underneath its canopy. Many communities now discourage planting Norway maples and encourage native alternatives like sugar maple or red oak.
compareHints: Norway maple differs from sugar maple by its milky leaf sap, earlier and more chartreuse spring flowers, and wider-angled seed wings. Red maple has smaller leaves with more pointed lobes and red flowers/stems. Silver maple has deeply cut leaves with silvery undersides, while Norway maple leaves are uniformly green on both sides.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red maple differs from sugar maple by its toothed leaf margins, red leaf stems, and earlier seed drop.
Unlike its maple relatives, striped maple has the distinctive white-striped bark that no other North American maple possesses.
Among New England's maples, sugar maples have the smoothest leaf edges (no teeth) and the most rounded lobe shapes, while red maples have serrated edges and more pointed lobes.
Box elder stands out dramatically from other New England maples because it's the only one with compound leaves instead of the classic lobed maple leaf shape.
Among New England's maples, mountain maple is the odd one out—it's the only one that stays truly shrubby and forms colonies rather than growing into a single-trunked tree.

Among New England maples, silver maple stands out for its deeply dissected leaves and silvery undersides - much more dramatic than the shallow lobes of red maple or the more rounded lobes of sugar maple.
Among New England maples, sycamore maple stands out for its exceptionally large leaves on long stalks and drooping flower clusters.
Among New England maples, Amur maple is unique for its consistently small size and three-lobed leaves with the distinctly elongated center lobe.

Japanese maple differs from all native New England maples by having much more deeply divided, delicate leaves with 5-9 narrow lobes compared to the broader, less-divided leaves of sugar maple, red maple, and silver maple.
Field maple is much smaller than sugar maple, red maple, or Norway maple, with distinctively small, thick, round-lobed leaves that set it apart from all other maples in New England.
